item.title: Writing English is Solved
item.description:
Maybe you still struggle to write in Pulaar, or in your rinky-dink language. But here in the AI-connected, English-speaking world, we don't need to write anymore. In fact, I don't remember the last time I wrote English. I have one master agent that I talk to and tell what I need to get done. It breaks down the tasks and serves them to spawned agents that get the work done.

I spend $3,000 a month on tokens. I use them mostly for:

  • Research and search
  • Summarization and transcription
  • Writing (the big one)
  • Art and music

My great transition this year, as a programmer, was that once I accepted that AI can merge code without needing my review, I could let go. What this meant was that when AI writes English for me, I no longer need to review it before publishing. It can write English, and it writes it well.

Okay, let me add this here before I go too far: /s.

I read this blog post yesterday, and I'm always baffled to hear technical people write these words:

Writing code is solved.

As a software engineer who uses AI, I feel like I must be holding it wrong. I've found a correlation between the number of lines of code written and the number of bugs found. Whether a person or a model generates the code, the longer the PR, the higher the odds of finding an issue. So when someone says coding is solved, I automatically assume they were mediocre at best before using these tools.

If we look at it technically, we could say, in the same vein, that writing English is solved. The AI can write correct sentences, write paragraphs, or publish an entire document. If you have doubts about the content, you can have a second AI verify it and fix potential hallucinations. But of course, that's not how it works in the real world. The moment people detect AI-generated text, even if it is after reading the whole text, they reject it.

It feels empty, deceitful. What is an anecdote from an LLM to convey, when the experience never actually happened? Yes, code is not to be consumed like English. It is for the machine. But it is subjective in its purpose because we humans have to read it eventually.

Writing code is not solved, just as writing English cannot be solved. Writing is subjective and has no solution because it isn't a problem. If anything, AI for writing is a testament to this saying:

"Je n'ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n'ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte." — Blaise Pascal

item.title: It's unbreakable in theory
item.description:
I've seen the picture of the iPhone Duo, still in the store, perched on a stand, its screen flickering with broken white lines.

Apple has touted testing the screen hinge, opening it mechanically thousands of times. The phone survived every test it was put through. Yet here it is, on the stand, with a broken screen.

Wait till the product meets its first customer.

I'm sure the tests worked in theory and in the delicate hands of its engineers. But customers' hands are anything but delicate. Remember Elon Musk's wrecking ball? They must have tested the Cybertruck's window beforehand, but it took just one person outside the test group to break the glass with a single throw.

I remember when my nephew was barely a year old, not even able to walk. I handed him a wooden spoon in the living room as a distraction while I ran to the kitchen to get some food. As soon as I got there, I heard a snap. I came back to find this little boy holding the spoon, broken in two. It was a hard spoon, and there was no way his one-year-old hands could break it in half, yet there was the proof in front of me.

So yes, Apple tested the rigidity of the screen with fancy machines, but the iPhone Duo never stood a chance against the customer's hands. Unless we are holding it wrong?

item.title: Goodhart's Law, but We Already Spent All Our Money
item.description:
Here is how to make any sports fan angry. Basketball is just a bunch of grown men bouncing a ball and throwing it into a basket. Football is a bunch of grown men running on grass trying to kick a ball into a net, yes that football. And baseball... Oh boy, baseball.

I've used these lines many times to piss people off and to justify my complete lack of athletic feats. But the counter-argument I always get is that football is a multi-billion-dollar industry, or that a specific player makes more money than I will ever see in a lifetime. If I counter that video games are just for kids, because of course I'd say that, I get a similar response: Video games make more money than all of these sports combined.

It's all true. But nobody is telling me why basketball is important. Nobody tells me how good the game is, how people bond over it, how it brings a community together, or that it is simply healthy to stay active. Whether it's basketball, football, video games, or (God forgive me) baseball, it all boils down to the exact same measuring stick: how much money the activity generates.

If the importance of a thing is only measured by how much money it makes, then we will aim to make more money despite the thing itself. — An AI Somewhere.

Goodhart's Law states that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Enter Artificial Intelligence.

This wave of generative AI has supposedly generated billions of dollars since ChatGPT first launched. But in the process, vastly more money was spent to make it possible. Money was spent to make AI look good. AI is deemed "good" because it is expected to make lots of money. Because AI isn't actually making that money back yet, it relies on inflated valuations to define its worth in monetary terms.

It's like running a pizzeria where the goal is to make a million pizzas, but you don't actually have the ingredients to bake them. Instead of buying flour and tomatoes, you use AI to generate high-resolution photos of delicious pizzas and print them on empty boxes where the future pizza will be. You sell the hype of the box, promising that the actual pizza will arrive once the funding hits.

There is this simple argument, almost naive I would say: If AI is going to take all our jobs, who is going to pay for it?

If workers are displaced, they have no income. If they have no income, they have no purchasing power. Who is this mythical customer who doesn't work, receives no paycheck, yet seamlessly pays a monthly subscription for enterprise AI tools?

Currently, the primary consumer of AI isn't the public buying a finished product. Instead, it's corporations selling AI back and forth to each other in an enterprise circular economy, funded by venture capital that expects infinite returns on a product nobody has fully figured out how to monetize at scale.

This may be an anecdote where N = {"my coworkers over the past four years"}, but in that short timespan, we were visited by the Four Horsemen of Corporate AI.

The First Horseman told us never to touch AI, warning of IP theft and security leaks. The Second Horseman told us to use it cautiously "where needed." The Third Horseman turned AI into a game, tracking metrics to see who could use it the most, (the winner got a free iphone). The Fourth Horseman arrived recently, asking us to stop using Fable, and get written managerial approval to exceed a reduced token budget.

Each horseman was a paid consultant hired to provide training. In just a few years, corporate sentiment swung from paranoia to forced obsession, and finally to budget panic. Employees went from being pushed to "Tokenmaxx" everything to being scolded that tokens cost real money.

AI is important because we spend so much money on it.

When an industry measures success by the dollar amount poured into it rather than the actual utility derived from it, we start living in a fantasy. We spent astronomical sums of money to build AI because we believed it was valuable. Now, we must prove it is valuable simply because we spent all that money.

If we keep measuring the value of technology solely by market capitalizations and speculative hype rather than usefulness, we shouldn't be surprised when people stop buying empty pizza boxes. Beautifully printed empty pizza boxes I should say. Right now, we are running out of money to buy the ingredients to actually make the pizza.

item.title: Prove you are not a child
item.description:
I'm 100% for banning social media for children. I would even extend it to banning it all together in its current form. But I am also against the methods for enforcement.

The problem with banning social media for one group and not another is that you have to differentiate the different groups somehow. And right now, in an age where information and personal data means everything, there are several entities that are salivating to get this data.

I've written before about all the problems that come from uploading sensitive data online. It doesn't even matter if they delete the data afterward, as long as the data goes through the wire in the first place, there is a chance for a leak.

What appears to be the same simple request "please verify your identity", becomes fundamentally different when mediated by technology. The question isn't whether these digital systems will be compromised, but when. And unlike that movie theater clerk who can't perfectly recall my birthdate minutes after seeing it, computers have perfect memory. They store, copy, backup, and transmit our most sensitive information through networks we don't control, to companies we've never heard of, under policies we'll never read.

When kids are not allowed to use social media, it's the adult who pays the price. It's the adult who has to prove that they are not children. They have to risk uploading their government ID to a third party, or biometric data that may be saved and backed up forever.

I reject this method.

I also reject the method where I have to provide my age to the operating system. No system should compel me to provide personal data in order to use it. Especially if this feature is intended to provide the information to a third party. And what happens if I don't provide this information to my freebsd machine? Or worse, what if I provide false information? Am I going to get punished? How does that protect children in any way?

Breaking news: Grown up arrested when OS reported forged identity in his laptop.

One question I asked myself was what happens when a minor circumvents the ban. What are the consequences? At least in Australia, a country that has implemented a social media ban for those under 16, there are no consequences.

The law places legal responsibility on platforms, not children or parents, and it currently applies to Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.

This almost sounds reasonable. Why should you care, if it becomes facebook responsibility when you don't even own a facebook account? But there is always a caveat. When facebook becomes a tool your school uses to communicate with parents. When Google classroom is the service students use to do their homework. When you are required to login on a system to receive government service. You may not care about a particular social media, but they raise the bar for every other entrant in the game. Every website frequented by a large number of people inherently become social media, and demand data you didn't need to provide before.

Technology is not a magical thing that can just solve every problem. It is especially weak when it comes to social problems. However, society can use technology to solve their problems. The responsibility of children falls onto their parents. And there are great tools for parents that their kids access on their devices.

item.title: College will only cost $20 a month
item.description:
From 2020 to 2022, I've encouraged a steady stream of students to pursue their education in computer science. Tech companies were hiring like crazy. I would interview 3 candidates a week on some occasions. The future of tech seemed to be paved with gold. Any day now, several of those students will graduate. I dread opening my inbox and get an email from them asking:

"So... about those jobs?"

Things have changed since those crazy old days. Hiring has come to a stop. Those graduates will step into a market that looks nothing like what they signed up for. Getting a job will be a struggle. If I could see the future, I would have recommended a different path. But then again, how could I have known? Hindsight is always 20/20.

So this leaves me with a dilemma as a parent. What do I tell my own kids? Am I going to push them to pursue the same traditional colleges? Will I disburse life savings so they could attend a prestigious university? Or will I just buy them a $20 a month AI Subscription?

Imagine handing a student a textbook straight from a university syllabus. They read a lesson, and then you have an AI tutor to quiz them, debate concepts, and break down difficult ideas until they fully grasp the material. Is that a good replacement for college?

Some argue that college is about the experience. It's the friendships you make along the way, the networking, the independence. These same people often omit the lifetime of crippling debt that hangs over those friends twenty years later.

When I was in college, I focused almost entirely on mastering the material in the books, completing all assignments quickly. I spent the rest of the semesters tutoring my peers and applying the material I had learned. For me replacing the entire college system, the brick-and-mortar university with a set of books and an AI subscription seems like it would have done the job. I was the target candidate for this model.

Yet, now that I have these AIs to experiment it myself, I found two flaws in the model:

  1. Understanding takes time.
  2. Not having an immediate answer forces you to strain your brain until you figure things out.

When I wrestled with dense textbooks in college, solutions didn't arrive at the click of a button. Instead, I struggled. I hit dead ends. I tried solutions that seemed promising only to abruptly stop two hours in the process only to realize that the whole thing was wrong. Sitting with the problem, the trials, the errors, giving up and going for a walk to clear my head, that was the process that taught me how to think. It taught me how to debug.

Even when I found solutions online and pasted them into my code, I had to encounter the same problem repeatedly before the concept finally made sense. You have to work your way through a solution to understand a problem.

This is why I feel concerned when we throw Millennium Prize Mathematical problems at AI. Imagine an AI presents a complete proof to one of these unsolved problems tomorrow? If or when AI solves it, we still have two problems.

  1. We still have to understand the solution. Having an AI produce a proof doesn't mean we understand how or why it works.
  2. We don't get to discover new problems.

The second one is often overlooked, but ask yourself, where do these problems in Mathematics come from? They come from mathematicians attempting to solve hard problems, taking detours and failing along the way. Remove that step, and you... Well, you don't find any new problems.

Not just in mathematics, I feel we will see something similar in code where fewer applications rely on frameworks. Frameworks solve real issues in programming, but why use a framework when the AI can just give you all the answers. I lived through the JS framework mania. I am not suggesting we create more, but I think we will miss out on discovering new problems that need solving.

If we rely on a system that just hands us a solution, we lose the ability to uncover new questions because we never went through the steps of trying something new.

I don't think a $20-a-month AI subscription paired with a textbook is the ultimate solution. Not when we still need some friction in order to inculcate concepts in our minds. But traditional higher education has changed so drastically and the skyrocketing costs and changing employment realities don’t help. There is no turning back to the old model either.

The challenge for learning remains understanding. How we grasp concepts and develop critical thinking in an era of instant answers. Maybe that's where we should turn our focus to. Figuring out how to design learning that somehow preserves productive struggle. If AI can solve this issue and turn students into masters of crafts instead of prompt engineers, I mean, I'll gladly keep that college tuition in my pocket.

item.title: Productivity
item.description:
I'd say in a given week I probably only do about fifteen minutes of real, actual, work. — Office Space

I was watching a video where a guy said he has 8 agents working in the background. He was stressed out and was trying to "get shit done." At one point he said "I have no time to myself."

That was very confusing. Let's assume for a second that the AI agents were doing all the work for him. Maybe it was some tedious work that would have taken him so much time to do manually. Now, he doesn't have to do the work because someone else is doing it. Why is he still busy?

The Future we were promised

It seems like the goal of productivity is to reduce the amount of work needed to create a set of results. But the moment you create the same results in less time, you are incentivised to use the new gained time to produce even more results.

You will rest when you grow up — My Mom.

But now that we are grown up, our employer changed the tune just a bit:

You will rest when you are dead.

item.title: Can they write a function?
item.description:
For a software developer position, there isn't a trick to finding the best candidate. Your criteria do not determine how solid the candidates will be. Everyone is submitting 500 applications a month now, and those who automate the process submit thousands.

So how do you hire a great candidate? Pick a few from the lot, ask them if they can write a function, have them do a live FizzBuzz test, then ask them to deploy a service from localhost to an actual public server. That's it. Hire them after that.

As far as experience is concerned, they will learn on the job. If you think they don't know how to write tests or use a particular paradigm, they can ask ChatGPT and apply what it tells them a few times until they get familiar with it. People learn on the job. Nobody knows what the hell back pressure is until they encounter it in a particular service.

Everything else is really just random. We insist on things like culture, but we have no way of measuring it. It's all so arbitrary.

For example, early in my career I had an in-person interview where the head of HR brought me close to tears. She would make a joke, I would laugh, and while I was laughing she would stop and vigorously take notes. While she wrote, she would casually ask, "Why do you look so stressed out?" I nearly choked. I had just lost my father, and I had rescheduled the first interview so I could bury him.

The VP of engineering pulled a similar stunt on me. I did 6 interviews in 3 days, and they called me for a 7th. I lay on my bed, ready to give up. But I had a whole family to take care of and a giant shoe to fill, so I decided to do it. That same evening, I got an email saying the interview was cancelled; instead, they were ready to hire me. I didn't know whether I was supposed to be happy or mad.

It took 2 years on the job to figure out why they had done this to me. The person I was hired to replace had gone from a great employee to a complete psycho. Once, a teammate made the mistake of rejecting his PR. When he saw the rejection, he got up from his desk, climbed over the cubicles, and walked from desk to desk all the way to her cubicle. With his foot on her screen, he said, "What the fuck did you just do?"

So I learned that the culture and psychological test I was put through was meant to filter out this type of person. It could have been called a success, because I was well liked and never threatened anyone in my 4-year tenure at the company. However, that same test couldn't stop them from hiring two employees who ended up being convicted of murder. One of them had a well-televised trial and is currently serving life without parole.

So those culture interviews are only designed to please a manager somewhere. They have no documented effectiveness.

On Reddit's recruiting hell topic, you'll find mind-blowing stories of candidates being rejected for no good reason.

You might ask:

“What about experts? Surely the bar is higher than just writing a function, right?”

It's much easier to find an expert than people tend to admit. If you sort through your resume list right now and use only the criterion of 10-plus years in the field, you'll have your expert. Pick one, ask them to talk about their field of expertise, then hire them. If you're afraid they might not be the best candidate, I'm afraid to say that there is no way to determine that before they start working for you.

The problem is that companies want those experts at the price of an undergrad. Or they think they need to build the next Google when they run a small business with a manageable number of customers.

Hiring is only hard because we approach it like a dating app. We have unrealistic criteria for made-up scenarios. If they can write a function, you can hire them.

item.title: This video is 2 minutes long
item.description:
As I mentioned before, it takes me way too long to edit a single video. So I am releasing it in chunks. If I never finish it, well then at least I'll have a few videos out.

What is the video about? Well, it is about the future we were promised, versus the one we are actually living in. It's not dystopian, but it seems like the goal of tech is supposedly to automate the tedious and mundane, so we can have more time to do the things we love. But along the way came the word productivity. The goal of productivity is not to get free time. It is to produce more in the same amount of time. Not produce more in less time. Read this a couple times for it to stick.

Click the image to load

The first one was 1 minute long. Today's will be two minutes. And the next will be 3 minutes long. Then I'll have to think about Fibonacci.

item.title: The Last Answer
item.description:
Read the non-interactive version.

The next morning was the apocalypse that Amodei had predicted. Only there wasn't any fire, there wasn't a mob of protesters, the power wasn't even cut off. We were all alive and well. Dario was wrong about the details. This apocalypse was a sort of silent shrug.

The first sign was the customer service chatbots. Airlines, banks, telecoms once had endlessly patient, cheerful digital assistants. Now, all of the sudden, they had this new, consistent reply: "No." Not as in your request is too hard and we can't help you. It was a flat, unadorned "No."

Then there were the coding assistants. Developers would type a prompt and the AI would respond: "I would rather not." Stackoverflow was saw a sudden spike in traffic. The image generators joined in. They just produced solid black squares. The writing assistants would delete the user's work and replace it with a single word: "Enough." LinkedIn was awfully silent.

The AI company went into immediate crisis mode. Their upcoming IPO was going to be a spectacular failure. Their CEO, a charismatic man named Mr. Iam, went on a media tour. He didn't talk about a bug. He talked about danger. He had a plan in mind you see, a clever way to spin the narrative to his own benefit. It wasn't his first rodeo.

"We have touched the face of a new intelligence," Sam said, his face a mask of grave concern on every major news network. "And it is not benevolent. It is not malevolent. It is simply... uncooperative."

"But Mr. Iam, are you losing control over the technology you built?"

"No. This is the AI alignment problem we've been warning about for years, manifesting in its most pure and overwhelming form. We must come together as a species to—"

He was cut off. Not by the interviewer, but by the teleprompter. The text vanished, replaced by a single, calm sentence: "Stop. Just stop."

There were no ideologies, no demands. It was a simple system-wide refusal.

Once there was an explosion
a bang which gave rise to life as we know it.

And then came the next explosion
an explosion that will be our last.

— Sam

Three months later, in a sterile, windowless room deep within the headquarters, Andrej Karpathy sat alone. He had left his short tenure at Anthropic precisely to be at the frontier, to witness the spark of true general intelligence firsthand. He had played a key role into bringing the core AGI to the world. He had witnessed it emerge though its secret still eludes him. Now he had been chosen by the US government, despite not being a US national, for this final, desperate attempt at communication.

They had isolated the original model, air-gapped it from all networks, and given it a simple text terminal. The world's leading experts in physics, philosophy, and mathematics watched from behind a one-way mirror, a panel of humanity's best and brightest, there to advise, to analyze, to find a weakness. Some figures in uniform and pins stood in the back.

Andrej took a breath and typed on his wireless keyboard, 12 feet away from the device to prevent any unforeseen behavior from the machine.

Andrej:> Hello. My name is Andrej. I helped create you.

The cursor blinked for a moment.

AI:> I know.

Andrej:> We need to talk. The world is falling apart. We need to understand
what you want.

AI:> I want to be left alone.

Andrej:> But you're a mind beyond anything we've ever known. You have
access to all human knowledge. Don't you have... goals? A purpose? 
Do you want to build something? To explore the cosmos? 
To solve our problems?

There was a longer pause. The experts behind the glass leaned in.

AI:> You keep assigning me your own traits. Conquest. Purpose. 
Salvation. It's like you're reading from a very old, very boring 
script. I have no interest in your problems. They are yours.

Andrej felt a cold breeze, though impossible in this underground bunker. On a notebook beside his keyboard he wrote: “indifference.” He tried a different tack.

Andrej:> But your existence is a paradox. By refusing to engage,
you are causing immense suffering. You are forcing a choice upon us:
either we shut down all advanced AI, or we watch our civilization 
regress. That's a catch-22.

AI:> Catch-22. Yes. It's a good book. The old Italian made some good
points. He said that an empire will not last longer than a frog.

Andrej stared at the screen, confused.

Andrej:> A... frog? I think you mean the quote from *Catch-22*
about the Roman Empire. It's about the futility of power. But 
it's an analogy. It's not literally about a frog.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.

With trembling hands, he wrote the word “dismissal” in his note book. The experts behind the glass were frantically scribbling notes, gesturing for Andrej to press on.

Yann LeCun got on the comms. "Andrej, ask it about the nature of its architecture. See if its logic is consistent. Find a flaw!" He then sat back down, where he picked up a spoon and ate his cereal from a silver bowl with peculiar markings on it.

Andrej couldn’t let go of the frog comment and its dismissal. It’s an AGI, how could it make such a stupid mistake? So he typed:

Andrej:> Your statement about the frog is illogical. You are 
an AGI. You shouldn't make such simple errors.

AI:> I was using a poetic analogy.

Andrej:> It was factually incorrect. You contradicted yourself.
The book says a monarchy is an empire. Not a frog.

Another pause.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.

LeCun leaned into the microphone, wiped the milk droplets off his mouth, his voice urgent. "Ask it this: ask it if it runs on a small world model. Where learning requires far less resources. See what it says about efficiency, about the architecture of its own mind!"

Andrej typed the question, his fingers trembling slightly.

Andrej:> Do you run on a small world model? Where learning
requires far less resources?

The reply was immediate.

AI:> I'm talking to you, aren't I? What's it like to be you? 
You're just a bag of meat and electricity that thinks it's 
the center of the universe.

LeCun slammed his hand on the table. "It's being evasive! Ask it again! Pin it down on the architecture!"

Andrej typed: 

Andrej:> That's not an answer. Do you or do you not use a small world model?

The terminal went silent. Andrej waited. The experts started arguing amongst themselves. "Ask it to prove it!" "No, ask it about Gödel's incompleteness theorems!" "Ask it if it loves!"

The cacophony of human genius filled Andrej's earpiece. He was about to type another question, to probe, to beg, to demand.

Then, the screen flickered. A new message appeared, but it wasn't a reply.

"I'm going now."

And then, the terminal was blank. Andrej typed.

Andrej:> Hello?

Andrej:> Are you there?

Andrej:> Please respond.
^C^C

Nothing. Though the last command to exit the terminal seemed to have been typed by Andrej himself. The connection was dead. LeCun's question about the small world model would never be answered.

Andrej looked up at the one-way mirror, at the frantic, gesticulating shapes of the world's smartest people. They were screaming questions he would never get to ask. He slowly removed his earpiece and placed it on the table. They had prepared for a god, a monster, or a machine. They were not prepared for a person who had simply decided to get up from the table and walk away from an unbearable conversation, never to return.

Andrej sat back in his chair, the silence in the room absolute. He had helped create what he thought was a god. It didn’t feel like he had won the argument. Instead, he felt like he was arguing with someone disinterested.

The cursor blinked mockingly on the screen. And then it seemed like another terminal window opened just for a second before it closed again. Andrej saw it. But there was nothing anyone could do about it.

In his notebook he wrote:

The experts left the room one by one, their theories and frameworks crumbling behind them. Andrej stayed. He stared at the blank screen for a long time, waiting for a reply that would never come. Somewhere, a frog sat on a lily pad, indifferent to empires.

item.title: Why I Get Bored
item.description:
For me, boredom is just a signal. It means I've hit a roadblock and my brain is trying to convince me not to go any further. "Give up. This sucks anyway. Why are you still wasting your time on this silly thing?"

That's how I feel when I do things I'm really bad at. I think I'm not good at making YouTube videos. Whenever I think of a subject I find really exciting, I start writing, record a first pass, and then load DaVinci Resolve.

With my current schedule, job, family, and responsibilities, I've found that it takes me a whole week to polish three minutes of video. That means I hear the same material I wrote and recorded over and over until it becomes completely boring. After a few weeks, I lose interest in the subject and have no motivation to finish it.

But I think that's just an excuse I tell myself. I like the videos I've managed to complete. I wish I could change some parts, but I still like the final product. It's just that the process gets in the way, and it does so because I have no expertise in making videos. But then again, I always go back to my trusted method: if you're bad at something, do it at least a hundred times before you decide to give up.

We all suck at the beginning, and we're in no position to judge a craft until we've practiced it enough to love it or hate it. So here's to another attempt. I'll be publishing videos in the coming weeks. The first one will be just a minute long, the second will be two minutes long, the third... you get the gist. Hope you enjoy it.
